quick.summary: How to stop users from clicking the same button twice.
quick.takeaway: Show users the system heard them immediately after they click.

parts.title: Give feedback right away

beats.line: Users submit the form twice. They get angry. How do we fix it?
By telling them you heard them. Do they know the form is working?
Think of a crosswalk button. What happens when you press it?
Right. In our field, that is visibility of system status.
Can I just say show immediate feedback?
Without a light, you might press the button three more times.
Because I might think it is broken. Just like our payment form?

parts.cliff: We need to show them what is happening next.

beats.line: Exactly. We have to show them that the system is doing the work.
So the moment they click, I should just disable the button?
Yes. But then what? Just leave them staring at a grey button?
I guess not. What should we show instead?
You swap the button text for a spinning circle.
Oh, so they know the form is actually processing.
Yes. It is a clear sign the computer is thinking.
I will disable the button and show a spinning circle to stop double clicks.
Give them a signal, and they will gladly wait.

quiz.question: A user clicks a save button. What is the best immediate response?
options: Change the button to say saving.
Wait until the file is completely saved.
Send an email confirming the save.
Log the click in the database.
quiz.explanation: Changing the button provides instant feedback, telling the user their action was received.

quiz.question: Showing that the system is working makes users less likely to click again.
quiz.explanation: Showing system status, like a spinning circle, reduces frustration and prevents them from clicking again.
